blocks.en: "For our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ." — Philippians 3:20
blocks.es_reference: "Mas nuestra ciudadanía está en los cielos, de donde también esperamos al Salvador, al Señor Jesucristo." — Filipenses 3:20

blocks.en: A Kingdom Not of This World
blocks.es_reference: Un Reino No de Este Mundo

blocks.en: Jesus stood before the most powerful political authority of His day and spoke words that have echoed through every generation since: "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36). This was not an evasion. It was a declaration. It was a line drawn between two orders of reality — one temporal, the other eternal.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús se paró ante la autoridad política más poderosa de Su día y habló palabras que han resonado a través de cada generación desde entonces: "Mi reino no es de este mundo" (Juan 18:36). Esto no fue una evasión. Fue una declaración. Fue una línea trazada entre dos órdenes de realidad — uno temporal, el otro eterno.

blocks.en: The kingdoms of this world are built upon structure and strength. They require borders to define them, laws to govern them, and force to preserve them. They rise through power and are sustained by it. Even at their best, they remain bound to the limitations of human authority.
blocks.es_reference: Los reinos de este mundo están construidos sobre la estructura y la fuerza. Requieren fronteras que los definan, leyes que los gobiernen y fuerza para preservarlos. Se levantan a través del poder y son sostenidos por él. Incluso en su mejor estado, permanecen ligados a las limitaciones de la autoridad humana.

blocks.en: The Kingdom of God is of an entirely different nature. It does not advance by conquest, nor is it preserved by violence. It has no borders because it cannot be contained. It has no army because it does not compel allegiance; it transforms the heart. It is not imposed from the outside, but born within.
blocks.es_reference: El Reino de Dios es de una naturaleza enteramente diferente. No avanza por conquista, ni se preserva por la violencia. No tiene fronteras porque no puede ser contenido. No tiene ejército porque no compele lealtad; transforma el corazón. No es impuesto desde afuera, sino nacido por dentro.

blocks.en: The danger arises when these two kingdoms are confused. When the Church forgets that her Lord refused a political throne, she begins to seek one herself. When she forgets that Christ conquered through the cross, she is tempted to conquer through power. Christian nationalism, in its false form, is precisely this confusion. It takes the language of faith and places it in the service of political identity, territorial interest, and national ambition.
blocks.es_reference: El peligro surge cuando estos dos reinos se confunden. Cuando la Iglesia olvida que su Señor rechazó un trono político, ella comienza a buscar uno para sí misma. Cuando ella olvida que Cristo conquistó a través de la cruz, es tentada a conquistar a través del poder. El nacionalismo cristiano, en su forma falsa, es precisamente esta confusión. Toma el lenguaje de la fe y lo coloca al servicio de la identidad política, el interés territorial y la ambición nacional.

blocks.en: The Church may live within the nations, pray for them, and serve within them. But she must never surrender her identity to them. The New Testament does not present the Church as the chaplain of the state, but as a pilgrim people whose first and last loyalty belongs to Christ.
blocks.es_reference: La Iglesia puede vivir dentro de las naciones, orar por ellas y servir dentro de ellas. Pero nunca debe rendir su identidad a ellas. El Nuevo Testamento no presenta a la Iglesia como el capellán del estado, sino como un pueblo peregrino cuya primera y última lealtad pertenece a Cristo.

blocks.en: From Nation to People — The Great Transition
blocks.es_reference: De Nación a Pueblo — La Gran Transición

blocks.en: There was a time when God's redemptive work was visibly tied to a nation. Israel stood as a people set apart, with defined land, law, and identity. Through them, God revealed His holiness and His purposes to the world. Yet even then, the calling of Israel was never meant to terminate upon itself. It was to be a light — a witness pointing beyond its own borders.
blocks.es_reference: Hubo un tiempo en que la obra redentora de Dios estaba visiblemente atada a una nación. Israel se levantaba como un pueblo apartado, con tierra, ley e identidad definidas. A través de ellos, Dios reveló Su santidad y Sus propósitos al mundo. Sin embargo, incluso entonces, el llamado de Israel nunca fue destinado a terminar en sí mismo. Era para ser una luz — un testimonio que apuntaba más allá de sus propias fronteras.

blocks.en: With the coming of Christ, that trajectory reaches its fulfillment and transformation. No new nation replaces Israel. No sacred geography is established. Instead, a people is formed — drawn from every tribe, every language, every land. The boundaries that once defined identity are dissolved in a greater reality. Citizenship is no longer a matter of birthplace but of new birth.
blocks.es_reference: Con la venida de Cristo, esa trayectoria alcanza su cumplimiento y transformación. Ninguna nación nueva reemplaza a Israel. Ninguna geografía sagrada es establecida. En cambio, un pueblo es formado — extraído de cada tribu, cada lengua, cada tierra. Las fronteras que una vez definieron la identidad se disuelven en una realidad mayor. La ciudadanía ya no es asunto del lugar de nacimiento sino del nuevo nacimiento.

blocks.en: The Church is not a nation among nations. She is a people within all nations, yet belonging fully to none of them. Her allegiance is not divided; it is redirected. This is why the New Covenant cannot be reduced to the political ambitions of modern states. Promises given within a specific covenantal setting must not be carelessly transferred to nations that neither stand in Israel's role nor bear Israel's covenantal identity.
blocks.es_reference: La Iglesia no es una nación entre naciones. Ella es un pueblo dentro de todas las naciones, sin pertenecer plenamente a ninguna de ellas. Su lealtad no está dividida; está redirigida. Por eso el Nuevo Pacto no puede ser reducido a las ambiciones políticas de los estados modernos. Las promesas dadas dentro de un contexto pactual específico no deben ser transferidas descuidadamente a naciones que ni están en el rol de Israel ni llevan la identidad pactual de Israel.

blocks.en: When Christians attempt to read their own country into biblical prophecy or national covenant language, they often commit a theological error. They blur the line between the temporary and the eternal, between type and fulfillment, between the people of one covenant and the multinational body of Christ under the New Covenant. The Church's calling is not to baptize a nation's myths, but to bear witness to the reign of Christ in every nation.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando los cristianos intentan leer su propio país en la profecía bíblica o en el lenguaje del pacto nacional, a menudo cometen un error teológico. Borran la línea entre lo temporal y lo eterno, entre el tipo y el cumplimiento, entre el pueblo de un pacto y el cuerpo multinacional de Cristo bajo el Nuevo Pacto. El llamado de la Iglesia no es bautizar los mitos de una nación, sino dar testimonio del reinado de Cristo en cada nación.

blocks.en: The Cross and the Sword
blocks.es_reference: La Cruz y la Espada

blocks.en: In the garden, when the moment of crisis arrived, Peter reached instinctively for the sword. It was the most natural response imaginable. Power meets power. Force answers force. But Christ intervened: "Put your sword back in its place" (Matthew 26:52).
blocks.es_reference: En el huerto, cuando llegó el momento de crisis, Pedro alcanzó instintivamente la espada. Era la respuesta más natural imaginable. El poder se encuentra con el poder. La fuerza responde a la fuerza. Pero Cristo intervino: "Vuelve tu espada a su lugar" (Mateo 26:52).

blocks.en: In that command, an entire theology is revealed. Jesus did not resist arrest. He did not call for defense. He did not justify retaliation. He chose instead the path that would lead to suffering, humiliation, and death — not because He lacked power, but because He refused to use it in that way.
blocks.es_reference: En ese mandato, toda una teología es revelada. Jesús no resistió el arresto. No llamó a defensa. No justificó la retaliación. Eligió en cambio el camino que llevaría al sufrimiento, la humillación y la muerte — no porque le faltara poder, sino porque rehusó usarlo de esa manera.

blocks.en: The cross is not merely the means of salvation; it is the pattern of the Kingdom. To follow Christ is to walk that same path — to relinquish the instinct to dominate, to retaliate, to secure oneself through force. It is to trust that the purposes of God are not advanced by violence, but by obedience.
blocks.es_reference: La cruz no es meramente el medio de salvación; es el patrón del Reino. Seguir a Cristo es caminar ese mismo camino — renunciar al instinto de dominar, de retaliar, de asegurarse a uno mismo por medio de la fuerza. Es confiar que los propósitos de Dios no se avanzan por la violencia, sino por la obediencia.

blocks.en: And yet, again and again, the Church has been tempted to reverse this pattern. The sword has been taken up in the name of the One who laid it down. Violence has been justified under the banner of righteousness. The language of faith has been used to sanctify the ambitions of men.
blocks.es_reference: Y sin embargo, una y otra vez, la Iglesia ha sido tentada a invertir este patrón. La espada ha sido tomada en el nombre de Aquel que la depuso. La violencia ha sido justificada bajo el estandarte de la justicia. El lenguaje de la fe ha sido usado para santificar las ambiciones de los hombres.

blocks.en: Even some of the great figures of Christian history reveal how easily zeal can harden into persecution. Before encountering the risen Christ, Saul sought to stamp out those he believed were in error. He was religious, certain, forceful, and wrong. In later centuries, both Martin Luther and John Calvin, for all their undeniable contributions, acted at points more like Saul before conversion than like the crucified Christ. Those who dissented could be suppressed, punished, or handed over to state power. That fact does not erase their theological importance, but it does remind us that truth can be defended in a manner profoundly unlike Christ.
blocks.es_reference: Incluso algunas de las grandes figuras de la historia cristiana revelan cuán fácilmente el celo puede endurecerse en persecución. Antes de encontrar al Cristo resucitado, Saulo buscaba erradicar a los que él creía estaban en error. Era religioso, seguro, contundente y estaba equivocado. En siglos posteriores, tanto Martín Lutero como Juan Calvino, por todas sus contribuciones innegables, actuaron en puntos más como Saulo antes de la conversión que como el Cristo crucificado. Los que disentían podían ser suprimidos, castigados o entregados al poder del estado. Ese hecho no borra su importancia teológica, pero nos recuerda que la verdad puede ser defendida de una manera profundamente diferente a Cristo.

blocks.en: Augustine, Just War, and the Burden of Power
blocks.es_reference: Agustín, la Guerra Justa y la Carga del Poder

blocks.en: The question of war is never merely theoretical. It confronts every society that bears responsibility for order, protection, and justice. Governments possess the authority to wield force, and with that authority comes the moral weight of its use. The Church, therefore, has long wrestled with whether such force can ever be justified.
blocks.es_reference: La pregunta de la guerra nunca es meramente teórica. Confronta a cada sociedad que lleva la responsabilidad del orden, la protección y la justicia. Los gobiernos poseen la autoridad de empuñar la fuerza, y con esa autoridad viene el peso moral de su uso. La Iglesia, por lo tanto, ha luchado por mucho tiempo con si tal fuerza puede ser justificada alguna vez.

blocks.en: Augustine approached this issue with sobriety rather than triumphalism. He did not glorify war; he regarded it as a tragic necessity within a fallen world. His concern was not to sanction violence, but to restrain it. From his reflections emerged what has come to be known as the just war tradition.
blocks.es_reference: Agustín abordó este asunto con sobriedad en lugar de triunfalismo. No glorificó la guerra; la consideró como una necesidad trágica dentro de un mundo caído. Su preocupación no era sancionar la violencia, sino restringirla. De sus reflexiones surgió lo que ha llegado a ser conocido como la tradición de la guerra justa.

blocks.en: Augustine's classic just war precepts, stated simply:
blocks.es_reference: Los preceptos clásicos de la guerra justa de Agustín, declarados simplemente:

blocks.en: Legitimate authority: war must be declared by a proper governing authority, not by private vengeance or mob zeal.
blocks.es_reference: Autoridad legítima: la guerra debe ser declarada por una autoridad gobernante apropiada, no por venganza privada o celo de turba.

blocks.en: Just cause: war must address a real wrong, such as defense against aggression, not conquest, pride, or gain.
blocks.es_reference: Causa justa: la guerra debe abordar una injusticia real, como la defensa contra la agresión, no la conquista, el orgullo o la ganancia.

blocks.en: Right intention: the true aim must be peace, justice, and the restraint of evil, not revenge, hatred, glory, or plunder.
blocks.es_reference: Intención recta: el verdadero objetivo debe ser la paz, la justicia y la restricción del mal, no la venganza, el odio, la gloria o el saqueo.

blocks.en: Last resort: peaceful remedies should be seriously pursued before force is used.
blocks.es_reference: Último recurso: los remedios pacíficos deben buscarse seriamente antes de usar la fuerza.

blocks.en: Proportionality: the force used must not exceed what is necessary to address the wrong.
blocks.es_reference: Proporcionalidad: la fuerza usada no debe exceder lo necesario para abordar la injusticia.

blocks.en: Protection of the innocent: non-combatants are not to be treated as legitimate targets.
blocks.es_reference: Protección del inocente: los no combatientes no deben ser tratados como blancos legítimos.

blocks.en: These principles were intended as moral boundaries. They were meant to impose restraint upon human violence in recognition of human fallenness. Yet history presents a sobering reality. Nations rarely submit themselves to these constraints with integrity. Causes are declared just because they serve national interest. Intentions are framed as noble after decisions have already been made. Civilian suffering is acknowledged, but ultimately accepted. What is meant to restrain violence is often repurposed to legitimize it.
blocks.es_reference: Estos principios fueron destinados como límites morales. Estaban destinados a imponer restricción sobre la violencia humana en reconocimiento de la caída humana. Sin embargo, la historia presenta una realidad sobria. Las naciones rara vez se someten a estas restricciones con integridad. Las causas son declaradas justas porque sirven al interés nacional. Las intenciones son enmarcadas como nobles después de que las decisiones ya han sido tomadas. El sufrimiento civil es reconocido, pero finalmente aceptado. Lo que está destinado a restringir la violencia a menudo es reutilizado para legitimarla.

blocks.en: Measured against these precepts, many wars fail badly. The record of modern powers shows repeated departures from Augustine's safeguards. Many historians and ethicists contend that American involvement in Vietnam and later military engagements in the Middle East failed to meet Augustine's standard — that they lacked a clear and morally coherent just cause in his sense, or fell short as genuine last resorts, proportionate uses of force, or careful protections of the innocent. Others disagree, arguing the causes were more just than critics allow. The pastor need not settle every case to see the pattern Augustine warned against: the language of security and stability can conceal deeper interests and wider ambitions, in any nation's wars.
blocks.es_reference: Medidas contra estos preceptos, muchas guerras fallan gravemente. El registro de los poderes modernos muestra repetidos apartamientos de las salvaguardas de Agustín. Muchos historiadores y eticistas sostienen que la participación estadounidense en Vietnam y los compromisos militares posteriores en el Medio Oriente no cumplieron el estándar de Agustín — que carecieron de una causa justa clara y moralmente coherente en su sentido, o no calificaron como últimos recursos genuinos, usos proporcionales de la fuerza, o protecciones cuidadosas del inocente. Otros discrepan, argumentando que las causas fueron más justas de lo que admiten los críticos. El pastor no necesita resolver cada caso para ver el patrón que Agustín advirtió: el lenguaje de seguridad y estabilidad puede ocultar intereses más profundos y ambiciones más amplias, en las guerras de cualquier nación.

blocks.en: What was designed as a restraint upon war has often been used as a sermon in favor of it. This does not expose a failure in Augustine's moral vision so much as it exposes the tendency of power to bend ethical language to its own purposes. The state says peace is the goal while preparing for domination. The state says justice is the cause while pursuing influence. In that setting, the Church must not become the chaplain who blesses what Christ would judge.
blocks.es_reference: Lo que fue diseñado como una restricción sobre la guerra a menudo ha sido usado como un sermón a favor de ella. Esto no expone un fracaso en la visión moral de Agustín tanto como expone la tendencia del poder a doblar el lenguaje ético a sus propios propósitos. El estado dice que la paz es la meta mientras se prepara para la dominación. El estado dice que la justicia es la causa mientras persigue la influencia. En ese contexto, la Iglesia no debe convertirse en el capellán que bendice lo que Cristo juzgaría.

blocks.en: 💡 Christ Among the Displaced: Jesus Himself was, for a season, a refugee — carried into Egypt as an infant to escape a murderous king (Matthew 2:13-15). He taught that whatever is done for "the least of these" — the hungry, the stranger, the prisoner — is done for Him (Matthew 25:35-40). Whatever a Christian concludes about the policy questions surrounding immigration, that identification with the poor and displaced is not optional for the disciple's heart.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 Cristo entre los desplazados: Jesús mismo fue, por una temporada, un refugiado — llevado a Egipto de niño para escapar de un rey asesino (Mateo 2:13-15). Enseñó que lo que se hace por "estos mis hermanos más pequeños" — el hambriento, el extranjero, el preso — se hace por Él (Mateo 25:35-40). Cualquiera que sea la conclusión de un cristiano sobre las cuestiones de política migratoria, esa identificación con el pobre y el desplazado no es opcional para el corazón del discípulo.

blocks.en: Citizenship, Conscience, and the Integrity of Faith
blocks.es_reference: Ciudadanía, Conciencia e Integridad de la Fe

blocks.en: The tension between the Church and the state is not resolved in theory. It is resolved in the life of the believer. A Christian may live under various governments, carry different passports, and participate responsibly in civic life. These realities are not insignificant. Yet they do not define ultimate identity. The believer's citizenship lies elsewhere.
blocks.es_reference: La tensión entre la Iglesia y el estado no se resuelve en teoría. Se resuelve en la vida del creyente. Un cristiano puede vivir bajo varios gobiernos, llevar diferentes pasaportes y participar responsablemente en la vida cívica. Estas realidades no son insignificantes. Sin embargo, no definen la identidad última. La ciudadanía del creyente está en otro lugar.

blocks.en: That is why one may say, in the truest and holiest sense, "I am a Christian nationalist," provided it means this and nothing less: my nation is the Kingdom of God. An American passport may describe travel. A Canadian residence may describe history. A home in Mexico may describe present life. But none of these identifies the soul. The Christian's deepest citizenship is not of this world.
blocks.es_reference: Por eso uno puede decir, en el sentido más verdadero y santo: "Soy un nacionalista cristiano", siempre que signifique esto y nada menos: mi nación es el Reino de Dios. Un pasaporte estadounidense puede describir viajes. Una residencia canadiense puede describir historia. Un hogar en México puede describir la vida presente. Pero ninguna de estas identifica el alma. La ciudadanía más profunda del cristiano no es de este mundo.

blocks.en: Roger Williams and the Freedom of Conscience: Few voices saw the danger of religious power more clearly than Roger Williams. He understood that faith cannot be coerced. Belief compelled by law is not faith; it is compliance. For that reason, he argued that the church must not encroach upon the rights of individual belief, and the state must not compel conscience. His concern was not to weaken Christianity, but to protect its integrity from political corruption.
blocks.es_reference: Roger Williams y la Libertad de Conciencia: Pocas voces vieron el peligro del poder religioso más claramente que Roger Williams. Entendió que la fe no puede ser coaccionada. La creencia compelida por la ley no es fe; es cumplimiento. Por esa razón, argumentó que la iglesia no debe usurpar los derechos de la creencia individual, y el estado no debe compeler la conciencia. Su preocupación no era debilitar el cristianismo, sino proteger su integridad de la corrupción política.

blocks.en: Whenever religion seeks to take over the state, it commonly speaks in the language of righteousness, but the deeper appetite is often power rather than the will of God. It is the spirit of Saul trying to stamp out Christians, convinced he is defending truth while opposing the work of Christ. When church and state join hands in coercion, persecution is never far behind.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando la religión busca apoderarse del estado, comúnmente habla en el lenguaje de la justicia, pero el apetito más profundo a menudo es el poder más que la voluntad de Dios. Es el espíritu de Saulo tratando de erradicar a los cristianos, convencido de que está defendiendo la verdad mientras se opone a la obra de Cristo. Cuando la iglesia y el estado se unen en la coerción, la persecución nunca está lejos.

blocks.en: The Witness of History and Costly Discipleship
blocks.es_reference: El Testimonio de la Historia y el Discipulado Costoso

blocks.en: The Witness of History: History confirms how easily this pattern repeats. In Nazi Germany, large segments of both Protestant and Catholic communities aligned themselves with Hitler and the state. National identity and social order were elevated above obedience to Christ. Only a few were willing to pay the true cost of discipleship. Among them stood Dietrich Bonhoeffer, whose witness reminds the Church that discipleship is not proven in sentiment, but in costly obedience.
blocks.es_reference: El Testimonio de la Historia: La historia confirma cuán fácilmente este patrón se repite. En la Alemania Nazi, grandes segmentos tanto de las comunidades protestantes como católicas se alinearon con Hitler y el estado. La identidad nacional y el orden social fueron elevados por encima de la obediencia a Cristo. Solo unos pocos estaban dispuestos a pagar el verdadero costo del discipulado. Entre ellos estaba Dietrich Bonhoeffer, cuyo testimonio recuerda a la Iglesia que el discipulado no se prueba en el sentimiento, sino en la obediencia costosa.

blocks.en: Economics and Obedience: The same conflict emerges when faith runs against financial interest. In the American South, slavery was not merely a social custom; it was an economic engine. Cotton depended upon it. Because it was profitable, many Christians justified it, muted the claims of conscience, and ignored the fact that all men bear the image of God and that in Christ there is neither slave nor free. Resistance grew more strongly in places where there was less economic need to preserve the institution. That raises a painful but necessary question: does economics trump faith?
blocks.es_reference: Economía y Obediencia: El mismo conflicto emerge cuando la fe se enfrenta al interés financiero. En el sur estadounidense, la esclavitud no era meramente una costumbre social; era un motor económico. El algodón dependía de ella. Porque era rentable, muchos cristianos la justificaron, silenciaron los reclamos de la conciencia e ignoraron el hecho de que todos los hombres llevan la imagen de Dios y que en Cristo no hay esclavo ni libre. La resistencia creció más fuertemente en lugares donde había menos necesidad económica de preservar la institución. Eso plantea una pregunta dolorosa pero necesaria: ¿la economía supera a la fe?

blocks.en: "Why do you call me, 'Lord, Lord,' and do not do the things that I say?" — Luke 6:46
blocks.es_reference: "¿Por qué me llamáis, Señor, Señor, y no hacéis lo que yo digo?" — Lucas 6:46

blocks.en: The Stranger and the Memory of Arrival: The treatment of the foreigner reveals another layer of this tension. Europeans came to a new land with a sense of divine mandate. They arrived as aliens and strangers seeking land, opportunity, safety, and a future. Yet the native peoples they encountered were often deprived of rights, stripped of land, and at times pressed toward forced conversion. Those who came as outsiders did not always show mercy to those already there.
blocks.es_reference: El Extranjero y la Memoria de la Llegada: El trato del extranjero revela otra capa de esta tensión. Los europeos vinieron a una nueva tierra con un sentido de mandato divino. Llegaron como extranjeros y peregrinos buscando tierra, oportunidad, seguridad y un futuro. Sin embargo, los pueblos nativos que encontraron a menudo fueron privados de derechos, despojados de tierra y a veces presionados hacia la conversión forzada. Aquellos que vinieron como forasteros no siempre mostraron misericordia a los que ya estaban allí.

blocks.en: Today, a poor Mexican living on a few pesos wants what fathers and mothers everywhere have always wanted: the ability to provide safely, healthily, and economically for their family. In that respect, he wants what many Europeans wanted when they came to a new land. Scripture does not teach the people of God to despise such a person or to forget that he, too, bears God's image; whatever a nation's laws require, believers are called to care for the stranger and the alien in their hearts, and not let a person's legal status close off their compassion.
blocks.es_reference: Hoy, un pobre mexicano viviendo con unos pocos pesos quiere lo que los padres y madres en todas partes siempre han querido: la capacidad de proveer segura, saludable y económicamente para su familia. En ese aspecto, él quiere lo que muchos europeos querían cuando vinieron a una nueva tierra. La Escritura no enseña al pueblo de Dios a despreciar a tal persona ni a olvidar que él también lleva la imagen de Dios; cualesquiera que sean las leyes de una nación, los creyentes están llamados a cuidar al extranjero y al forastero en su corazón, sin dejar que el estatus legal de una persona cierre su compasión.

blocks.en: Immigration policy itself involves real, legitimate questions of law, security, and national sovereignty that Scripture does not resolve in detail, and Christians of good conscience weigh those questions differently. What Scripture does settle is the disposition of the heart: contempt for the foreigner has no place in a follower of Christ, whatever position a believer reaches on the policy questions themselves.
blocks.es_reference: La política migratoria en sí misma involucra preguntas reales y legítimas de ley, seguridad, y soberanía nacional que la Escritura no resuelve en detalle, y cristianos de buena conciencia sopesan esas preguntas de manera diferente. Lo que la Escritura sí establece es la disposición del corazón: el desprecio al extranjero no tiene lugar en un seguidor de Cristo, sea cual sea la postura que un creyente adopte sobre las cuestiones de política.

blocks.en: Patriotism Under Christ
blocks.es_reference: Patriotismo Bajo Cristo

blocks.en: Patriotism Under Christ: Love of country may express gratitude and civic responsibility, but patriotism cannot redefine righteousness. No nation's slogans or ambitions can be baptized as God's own cause; no modern nation stands as the exclusive vessel of His purposes. Patriotism does not justify becoming unlike Christ. It cannot excuse cruelty, sanctify pride, or bless conduct that contradicts the Savior whose kingdom is not of this world.
blocks.es_reference: Patriotismo Bajo Cristo: El amor al país puede expresar gratitud y responsabilidad cívica, pero el patriotismo no puede redefinir la justicia. Ningún lema ni ambición de una nación puede bautizarse como la causa misma de Dios; ninguna nación moderna se levanta como el vehículo exclusivo de Sus propósitos. El patriotismo no justifica volverse desemejante a Cristo. No puede excusar la crueldad, santificar el orgullo o bendecir conducta que contradice al Salvador cuyo reino no es de este mundo.

blocks.en: When national loyalty and obedience to Christ come into conflict, the path is not unclear. Christ is Lord. The believer belongs first and finally to Him.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando la lealtad nacional y la obediencia a Cristo entran en conflicto, el camino no es ambiguo. Cristo es Señor. El creyente pertenece primero y finalmente a Él.

blocks.en: Final Summary
blocks.es_reference: Resumen Final

blocks.en: The doctrine of the Church, the State, and Christian Nationalism teaches us that the Kingdom of God is not of this world. The Church is a people within all nations, but her ultimate allegiance is to Christ, not to any earthly flag. While we honor earthly authorities and participate in civic life, we must never confuse the Kingdom of God with any nation. The cross is the pattern of the Kingdom — sacrifice, not conquest. Augustine's just war tradition reminds us that even necessary force must be restrained by moral boundaries. History warns us that when the church aligns too closely with state power, persecution follows. Roger Williams called for a wall of separation to protect the integrity of faith. And the example of Jesus Himself — who was Himself, for a season, a refugee, and who identified Himself with the stranger and the displaced — calls us to care for the outsider, resist the temptation of nationalism, and remember that our true citizenship is in heaven. Christ is Lord. The believer belongs first and finally to Him.
blocks.es_reference: La doctrina de la Iglesia, el Estado y el Nacionalismo Cristiano nos enseña que el Reino de Dios no es de este mundo. La Iglesia es un pueblo dentro de todas las naciones, pero su lealtad última es a Cristo, no a ninguna bandera terrenal. Mientras honramos las autoridades terrenales y participamos en la vida cívica, nunca debemos confundir el Reino de Dios con ninguna nación. La cruz es el patrón del Reino — sacrificio, no conquista. La tradición de la guerra justa de Agustín nos recuerda que incluso la fuerza necesaria debe ser restringida por límites morales. La historia nos advierte que cuando la iglesia se alinea demasiado cerca con el poder del estado, la persecución sigue. Roger Williams llamó a un muro de separación para proteger la integridad de la fe. Y el ejemplo de Jesús mismo — quien fue, por una temporada, un refugiado, y quien se identificó con el extranjero y el desplazado — nos llama a cuidar al forastero, resistir la tentación del nacionalismo y recordar que nuestra verdadera ciudadanía está en los cielos. Cristo es Señor. El creyente pertenece primero y finalmente a Él.

blocks.en: "For our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ." — Philippians 3:20
blocks.es_reference: "Mas nuestra ciudadanía está en los cielos, de donde también esperamos al Salvador, al Señor Jesucristo." — Filipenses 3:20

mc.stem: According to John 18:36, what did Jesus explicitly say about His kingdom?
options: It is not of this world
It belongs first to Israel alone
It must be defended by force
It would soon replace Rome politically
mc.why: Jesus stated that His kingdom is not of this world, distinguishing His reign from earthly political systems.

mc.stem: What is the main theological error of false Christian nationalism according to this unit?
options: It rejects all forms of historical theology
It ignores all civil responsibility
It collapses the distinction between the Kingdom of God and earthly nations
It denies that God cares about justice
mc.why: The unit argues that false Christian nationalism wrongly merges Christ's kingdom with the ambitions and identity of the state.

mc.stem: Under the New Covenant, the people of God are primarily defined by:
options: Shared ethnicity and land
Faith in Christ
Political sovereignty
Military loyalty
mc.why: The Church is drawn from every tribe and nation and is defined by faith in Christ, not by ethnicity or geography.

mc.stem: What did Jesus tell Peter in the garden?
options: Put your sword back in its place
Defend the innocent by any means
Wait for a larger army
Take up your sword for the kingdom
mc.why: Matthew 26:52 is central in this unit because Jesus rebuked violent defense in His own cause.

mc.stem: What does the unit say the cross is, beyond being the means of salvation?
options: A temporary stage before political rule
A symbol of national identity
A pattern of the Kingdom
A reminder of Roman law
mc.why: The unit teaches that the cross is also the pattern of the Kingdom: sacrifice, obedience, and suffering rather than coercion.

mc.stem: How does the unit describe some of the behavior of Luther and Calvin toward dissenters?
options: Similar in some respects to Saul before his conversion
Entirely unrelated to state power
A model of religious liberty
Always fully consistent with enemy-love
mc.why: The unit notes that their use of coercive power at points resembled Saul's persecuting zeal more than the spirit of Christ.

mc.stem: Which of the following is one of Augustine's just war precepts?
options: War should increase national glory
War must be declared by legitimate authority
War should be pursued whenever interests are threatened
Civilian casualties are unavoidable and morally irrelevant
mc.why: Legitimate authority is one of the classic just war conditions associated with Augustine's framework.

mc.stem: Which is NOT one of Augustine's just war principles as presented in the unit?
options: Proportionality
Right intention
Last resort
Economic advantage
mc.why: Economic advantage is not a just war principle. The unit presents it as one of the ways nations often corrupt moral reasoning.

mc.stem: How does the unit describe the ongoing debate over American involvement in Vietnam and the Middle East?
options: As clearly just wars with no dispute
As morally neutral conflicts
As wars many historians argue fell short of Augustine's standards, though others disagree
As wars required by biblical prophecy
mc.why: The unit presents this as a genuine historical debate, using Augustine's criteria as the framework for weighing the question rather than a settled verdict.

mc.stem: What concern did Roger Williams emphasize?
options: Faith grows best through state enforcement
National religion is the highest form of unity
The church should govern the conscience by civil power
The church must not encroach on the rights of individual belief
mc.why: Roger Williams argued that conscience must not be coerced and that church and state should not dominate one another.

mc.stem: When religion seeks to take over the state, the unit says the deeper goal is often:
options: Neutral citizenship
Careful discipleship
Pure evangelism
Power rather than God's will
mc.why: The unit warns that religious control of the state often masks a desire for power rather than humble obedience to God.

mc.stem: What happened in Nazi Germany according to the unit?
options: The church became more committed to liberty
The state stopped using religion
Most churches rejected Hitler immediately
Both Protestant and Catholic communities often aligned with the state
mc.why: The unit points to widespread alignment with Hitler among both Protestants and Catholics, with only a few resisting at great cost.

mc.stem: Why did many Christians in the American South justify slavery?
options: Because abolition was forbidden by law everywhere
Because Scripture clearly commands race-based slavery
Because it had no economic significance
Because economic benefit distorted moral judgment
mc.why: The unit argues that slavery's profitability led many to justify what contradicted the image of God and Christian equality.

mc.stem: Which biblical truth is used in the unit against slavery?
options: Faith depends on class hierarchy
All men are made in the image of God and in Christ there is neither slave nor free
Slavery is necessary for order
The Old Testament cancels the New Testament
mc.why: The unit grounds its critique in the image of God and the New Testament teaching that in Christ there is neither slave nor free.

mc.stem: How does the unit compare poor Mexican migrants with earlier European settlers?
options: They want the same basic things: safety, provision, and a future for their families
One group is biblical and the other is not
Their situations cannot be compared morally
They are motivated by entirely different desires
mc.why: The unit stresses the shared human desire for family welfare and exposes the inconsistency of praising one migration story while condemning another.

mc.stem: What does Scripture command regarding the stranger and the alien, according to the unit?
options: Use them for labor
Care for them rather than oppress them
Treat them only according to economic value
Ignore them
mc.why: The unit emphasizes the biblical command to care for the stranger and alien rather than dehumanize or discard them.

mc.stem: Why does Christ's own experience as a refugee (Matthew 2:13-15) matter in this unit?
options: It claims citizenship laws never matter at all
It suggests Jesus supported modern bureaucracy
It grounds the call to compassion for the stranger in Christ's own life, not merely a principle
It denies the incarnation
mc.why: Christ's own flight into Egypt grounds the call to compassion for the displaced in His own experience, not an abstract rule.

mc.stem: What does the unit say about a nation's slogans or ambitions being treated as God's own cause?
options: They should be declared by God in Scripture
They are a harmless synonym for discipleship
No nation's slogans or ambitions can be baptized as God's own cause
They are the central confession of the Church
mc.why: The unit explicitly rejects the idea that God has given any modern nation a divine first-place status.

mc.stem: What limit does the unit place on patriotism?
options: Patriotism must remain under the lordship and character of Christ
Patriotism requires hostility to outsiders
Patriotism can replace obedience to Christ
Patriotism justifies being unlike Christ
mc.why: The unit teaches that patriotism cannot redefine righteousness or excuse conduct that contradicts Christ.

mc.stem: What is the final allegiance of the believer according to this unit?
options: To ethnic identity
To Christ and His Kingdom
To economic advantage
To whichever state offers the most security
mc.why: The conclusion of the unit is that Christ is Lord, and the believer belongs first and finally to Him.

fill.prompt: "For our ____ is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ" (Philippians 3:20).

sa.prompt: Analyze the statement "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36). What does it teach about the relationship between Christ's reign and earthly political power?
sa.model: The unit treats Jesus' words in John 18:36 not as an evasion but as a declaration. By saying His kingdom is not of this world, Christ drew a line between two orders of reality, one temporal and one eternal. His reign does not operate by the means of earthly political power and is not in competition for a throne in the ordinary political sense. This teaches that Christ's kingdom is of a different kind and source than the kingdoms of this world; it does not advance by force, conquest, or the machinery of the state. The relationship, then, is one of distinction: earthly political power belongs to a passing temporal order, while Christ's reign belongs to an eternal order that cannot be reduced to or captured by any nation or government. The kingdom of God is not a political program but a higher and lasting rule.

sa.prompt: Explain the "Great Transition" from national Israel to the multinational Church. Why is this significant for understanding Christian nationalism?
sa.model: The unit describes the Great Transition as the move from a time when God's redemptive work was visibly tied to a single nation to the era of the multinational Church. Israel stood as a people set apart, with a defined land, law, and national identity. Through Christ, God's people are no longer one nation but a community drawn from every nation, the Church. This transition is significant for understanding Christian nationalism because it means no single modern nation now occupies the place Israel once held. God's people are now multinational, so no country can claim to be God's chosen nation in the way Israel was. Christian nationalism errs precisely by trying to bind God's purposes to one country, ignoring the transition by which the people of God became a worldwide body. Recognizing the transition guards against confusing loyalty to a nation with loyalty to the kingdom of God.

sa.prompt: Explain Jesus' command to Peter to put away the sword (Matthew 26:52). What does it reveal about the kingdom's attitude toward violence?
sa.model: The unit recounts how Peter reached for the sword in Jesus' defense, calling it the most natural response imaginable, the instinct by which power meets power and force answers force. But Christ intervened, telling Peter to put his sword back in its place. This reveals the kingdom's fundamental attitude toward violence. Christ's kingdom does not advance by the sword; it does not establish or defend itself through coercion and bloodshed. At the very moment when violence seemed most justified, in defense of the Lord Himself, Jesus refused it. The lesson is that the means of the kingdom are not the means of worldly power. Where earthly kingdoms rise and protect themselves by force, Christ's kingdom rejects that path. This sets a pattern: the people of the kingdom cannot rightly use violence and coercion to advance God's cause, because their King explicitly disowned the sword as His instrument.

sa.prompt: Explain Augustine's just war precepts. What was his intention in developing them, and how have they often been misused?
sa.model: The unit presents Augustine's classic just war precepts, which include requirements such as legitimate authority, a just cause, right intention, war as a last resort, proportionality, and protection of the innocent. Augustine approached the question of war with sobriety rather than enthusiasm, and his intention was to set moral boundaries that would restrain war, treating these precepts as limits meant to hold violence in check. Measured against them, the unit notes, many wars fail badly. The misuse comes when what was designed as a restraint upon war is turned into a justification for it. Instead of using the precepts to question and limit conflict, people invoke them to bless wars they have already decided to fight. So Augustine's careful boundaries, intended to make war harder to justify, have often been twisted into a checklist for excusing it. The original purpose was restraint; the common abuse is to use them as permission.

sa.prompt: What did Roger Williams mean by the "wall of separation" between church and state? Why did he believe this protected the integrity of faith?
sa.model: The unit presents Roger Williams as one who saw the danger of religious power with unusual clarity. He understood that faith cannot be coerced, and he built his wall of separation to protect the integrity of faith. His point was not to shield the state from religion but to shield faith from the corrupting grasp of state power. When religion seeks to take over the state, or when the state enforces religion, faith is damaged, because genuine faith must be free and uncoerced; forced belief is not true belief at all. The wall of separation guards the conscience by keeping the coercive power of government out of the realm of belief, so that faith remains authentic rather than compelled. Williams believed that whenever religion seeks to seize political power it corrupts itself, so the separation actually preserves the purity and integrity of faith rather than threatening it.

sa.prompt: How does the unit use the example of Dietrich Bonhoeffer? What does his witness teach about costly discipleship?
sa.model: The unit uses Dietrich Bonhoeffer as a witness from history that reminds the Church discipleship is not proven in sentiment but in costly obedience. Bonhoeffer lived in a time when the pressure to align faith with national and political power was intense, and his witness stands as an example of refusing that pressure at great personal cost. His life teaches that following Christ is not merely a matter of warm feelings or verbal agreement; it is tested when obedience to Christ comes into conflict with the demands of the state and the surrounding culture. Costly discipleship means staying faithful to Christ even when that faithfulness is dangerous and demands real sacrifice. Bonhoeffer's example warns against a cheap, sentimental faith that costs nothing, and calls believers to the kind of obedience that holds firm to Christ's lordship above national loyalty, whatever the price.

sa.prompt: How does the unit connect economic interests to moral compromise? Use the example of slavery in the American South.
sa.model: The unit connects economic interest to moral compromise through the example of slavery in the American South. There, slavery was not merely a social custom but an economic engine; cotton depended upon it, and it was highly profitable. Because it was so profitable, many Christians justified it, muting the clear claims of conscience and Scripture in order to protect their economic advantage. The lesson is that economic self-interest has a powerful way of bending moral judgment. When obedience to God would threaten profit, there is strong temptation to rationalize wrong, soften convictions, and find religious cover for what benefits us financially. The example shows how easily faith can be compromised when money is at stake, and it warns believers that wherever economic interest collides with obedience to Christ, the pressure to justify sin for the sake of gain is real and must be resisted.

sa.prompt: What does Christ's own experience as a displaced refugee signify, and how does it challenge Christian nationalism?
sa.model: As an infant, Christ Himself was carried into Egypt to escape a murderous king, becoming for a season a refugee and a stranger in a foreign land. He later taught that whatever is done for the least of these — the hungry, the stranger, the prisoner — is done for Him. This grounds the call to compassion for the displaced in Christ's own life rather than an abstract rule, and it challenges Christian nationalism by showing that a faith fused too tightly with national identity or policy can grow cold toward the very people Christ identified Himself with. It does not settle the policy questions surrounding immigration, which believers may weigh differently, but it does mean that contempt for the stranger has no place in a follower of Christ.

sa.prompt: What does the unit teach about the proper limits of patriotism? How can a Christian love their country without idolizing it?
sa.model: The unit teaches that patriotism has proper limits because it cannot redefine righteousness. It states plainly that God never declared any nation first, and that no modern nation stands as the exclusive vessel of His purposes. Patriotism crosses its limit when it begins to justify what God condemns or to claim God's special favor for one country above all others. A Christian can love their country without idolizing it by keeping that love in its proper place, under the lordship of Christ rather than above it. Loving one's nation is not wrong, but it becomes idolatry when national loyalty is treated as ultimate, when the nation is exalted as God's chosen above the multinational people of God, or when patriotism is used to excuse injustice. The believer loves their country rightly by refusing to let it redefine right and wrong, holding ultimate loyalty to the kingdom of God.

sa.prompt: Summarize the main point of this unit. How should Christians relate to the state while maintaining ultimate loyalty to the Kingdom of God?
sa.model: The main point of the unit is that Christ's kingdom is not of this world, so believers must keep their ultimate loyalty to the Kingdom of God above every earthly nation and power. Through the Great Transition, God's people became a multinational Church, so no single country can claim Israel's old place or be treated as God's chosen nation. The kingdom does not advance by the sword, as Christ showed when He told Peter to put it away; faith cannot be coerced, as Roger Williams saw; and economic interest, national pride, and political power all tempt the Church to compromise, as slavery, Christ's own life as a displaced refugee, and Bonhoeffer's costly witness illustrate. Christians should therefore relate to the state with respect in its proper place but never with the supreme allegiance owed to Christ alone. They may love their country without idolizing it, obey lawful authority while refusing to let patriotism redefine righteousness, and keep conscience free, holding firm to the kingdom of God as their highest loyalty.
